data.reference_solution:
def buildTree(preorder, inorder):
    if not preorder or not inorder:
        return None
    root_val = preorder[0]
    root = TreeNode(root_val)
    mid = inorder.index(root_val)
    root.left = buildTree(preorder[1:1+mid], inorder[:mid])
    root.right = buildTree(preorder[1+mid:], inorder[mid+1:])
    return root
data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    vals = list(range(n))
    rng.shuffle(vals)
    def make_tree(lst):
        if not lst:
            return None
        mid = len(lst) // 2
        root = TreeNode(lst[mid])
        root.left = make_tree(lst[:mid])
        root.right = make_tree(lst[mid+1:])
        return root
    root = make_tree(vals)
    def get_pre(node, acc):
        if not node: return
        acc.append(node.val)
        get_pre(node.left, acc)
        get_pre(node.right, acc)
    def get_in(node, acc):
        if not node: return
        get_in(node.left, acc)
        acc.append(node.val)
        get_in(node.right, acc)
    pre, ino = [], []
    get_pre(root, pre)
    get_in(root, ino)
    return [pre, ino]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    vals = list(range(n))
    return [vals, vals]

data.pattern: Recursive Divide and Conquer with Hash Map
data.pattern_summary: This pattern involves breaking a problem down into smaller self-similar subproblems by identifying structural properties of data, often optimized using auxiliary memory like hash maps to quickly locate indices.

pattern_options.name: Recursive Divide and Conquer with Hash Map
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We repeatedly split the arrays into left and right subtrees based on the root position found via a hash map.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers work well for linear scans from both ends, but tree traversals require hierarchical splitting.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. BFS processes a tree level by level, whereas traversals define hierarchical parent-child relationships that match better with depth-first recursion.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. There are no overlapping subproblems being repeatedly computed to store in a table here.

signals.hint: Each traversal offers complementary structural information: preorder gives the root first, and inorder separates left and right subtrees.

signals.phrase: Each value in both arrays is unique
signals.hint: Uniqueness guarantees that every value maps to one exact position in the inorder traversal without ambiguity.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach takes the first element of the preorder list as the root, searches for that element's index in the inorder list using a linear scan, and then recursively builds the left and torch subtrees by slicing both lists.
data.brute_force_why: For every node in the tree, we slice the lists and call inorder.index(), which takes O(n) time per recursive step across n total nodes.
data.bottleneck: Using the list index method performs a linear scan every single time to find the root position, repeating work that could be avoided.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the position of the root is found in the inorder list.
Consider what happens to the cost of finding that index as the tree size grows.
Think about which data structure allows O(1) lookups for values instead of scanning a list.
data.brute_force_code:
def buildTree(preorder, inorder):
    if not preorder or not inorder:
        return None
    root_val = preorder[0]
    root = TreeNode(root_val)
    mid = inorder.index(root_val)
    root.left = buildTree(preorder[1:1+mid], inorder[:mid])
    root.right = buildTree(preorder[1+mid:], inorder[mid+1:])
    return root

data.overview: This algorithm constructs a binary tree from preorder and inorder traversal arrays using divide and conquer. The first element of any preorder segment is always the root, and we use a hash map to quickly locate this root in the inorder array to split left and right subtrees.
data.intuition: Imagine reading the root off the front of a book chapter, then looking at the table of contents to see exactly how many pages belong to the left and right subchapters.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach searches the inorder list using index() at every recursive step, turning the search into an O(n) operation inside a tree traversal. The optimized solution precomputes a hash map of every value and its index upfront on line 3, allowing each root lookup in the recursive helper to execute in O(1) time.

derivation.note: Builds the lookup dictionary once by iterating through the inorder list of size n.

derivation.cost: O(1) per call, called n+1 times
derivation.note: Base case check executes constant work at each of the n nodes and null leaves.

derivation.cost: O(1) per call, called n times
derivation.note: Hash map lookup retrieves the root index instantly instead of searching.

derivation.cost: O(1) per call, called n times
derivation.note: Recursive call for the left subtree processes a slice defined by indices without copying arrays.

derivation.cost: O(1) per call, called n times
derivation.note: Recursive call for the right subtree processes a slice defined by indices without copying arrays.

data.time_summary: Line 3 takes O(n) time to build the hash map. The helper function runs once per node (n times), performing O(1) operations at each node. Thus, the total time complexity is O(n), which matches the measured wall-clock growth of n^1.09.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because of the hash map storing n elements and the recursive call stack growing up to O(n) depth for a skewed tree.
data.takeaway: When a recursive algorithm repeatedly searches an array to find splitting points, precompute those indices in a hash map before starting the recursion.
mistakes: Slicing the preorder and inorder arrays directly instead of using index pointers, which reintroduces O(n^2) time and space overhead.
Off-by-one errors when calculating the left_subtree_size and passing boundaries into the recursive helper calls.
Forgetting to handle the base case where start pointers exceed end pointers, resulting in infinite recursion.
